value.overview: The Muscovy Duck is a large tropical duck native to Mexico, Central America, and South America. It is the only living species in the genus Cairina and has been domesticated widely for meat and eggs. Wild birds are associated with forested wetlands, rivers, lagoons, marshes, and estuaries, while domestic and feral birds may occur around farms, gardens, and urban ponds. The species is generally quiet compared with many other ducks.
value.classification: The Muscovy Duck belongs to the duck, goose, and swan family Anatidae. Its scientific name is Cairina moschata. Wild and domestic forms are commonly treated as the same species, although domestic birds show substantial variation in size and appearance.
value.identification: This is a large, heavy-bodied duck with a long tail, broad wings, and relatively long claws. Wild birds are mostly blackish with bold white wing patches, while females are smaller and duller. Both sexes have bare red or pink skin around the eyes and bill; males usually have larger facial caruncles. Domestic birds can be white, pied, brown, or highly variable and may look unlike wild individuals.
value.rangeHabitat: The Muscovy Duck occurs naturally from Mexico through Central America and across much of tropical South America. In Costa Rica it is a resident species, recorded locally in suitable lowland and foothill wetlands rather than as a regular migrant. It uses wooded streams, rivers, swamps, lagoons, estuaries, marshes, and small forest pools. In the country, sightings may involve wild birds as well as domestic or feral individuals near farms and settlements.
value.migrationStatus: Non-migratory. In Costa Rica, Muscovy Ducks are generally present year-round, with local movements between feeding, roosting, and breeding wetlands. Domestic and feral birds may also appear in places outside the species’ usual wild habitat.
value.breeding: Muscovy Ducks nest in tree cavities, hollow trunks, dense vegetation, or other sheltered sites close to water. The female usually lays a large clutch of pale eggs and incubates them alone, while the male may remain nearby. Ducklings are precocial and leave the nest soon after hatching. In tropical regions, breeding can occur during different parts of the year, often influenced by rainfall and local water conditions.
value.dietFeeding: The species has a varied diet that includes aquatic plants, seeds, fruits, grasses, grain, insects, small crustaceans, and other invertebrates. It feeds by grazing on land, dabbling in shallow water, and probing mud or vegetation. Muscovy Ducks often forage along stream edges and wet forest margins, and domestic or feral birds readily exploit food provided around farms, parks, and residences.
value.behavior: Muscovy Ducks are usually quiet and spend time resting on banks, low branches, fallen logs, or vegetation near water. They are strong fliers and can perch in trees, unlike many heavier domestic ducks. Birds may occur singly, in pairs, or in small groups. Males commonly defend space around females, while females lead ducklings between nesting, feeding, and shelter areas. They may become accustomed to people where domesticated.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be decreasing, but the species remains widespread and relatively abundant across much of its range.
